entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Johann V Thurzo (d. 1520), scion of the immensely wealthy Thurzo family, served as the Prince-Bishop of Wrocław (Breslau) in Silesia, a region now part of Poland, from 1506 until his death. Emerging from a lineage that controlled vast mining and metallurgical enterprises across Central Europe in partnership with the Fugger banking dynasty, Thurzo leveraged his family's immense fortune and intellectual pedigree to transform his episcopal see into a vibrant center of Renaissance humanism and artistic patronage. His tenure occurred at a pivotal moment, bridging the late medieval period with the burgeoning intellectual and religious ferment of the early Reformation.

Educated at the University of Kraków, a renowned hub for humanists, Thurzo cultivated an extensive network of scholars, artists, and reformers. He actively supported figures like Desiderius Erasmus, Albrecht Dürer, and Lucas Cranach the Elder, commissioning artworks, fostering intellectual discourse, and promoting educational initiatives within his diocese. His progressive outlook extended to ecclesiastical administration, where he sought to address corruption and spiritual laxity within the church, embodying a spirit of reform that resonated with many contemporary critics of the established order, including early proponents of the Reformation.
